title: Still higher derivatives — Taylor polynomials
goal: Build degree-$n$ Taylor polynomials $T_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x - a)^k$ that match a function's first $n$ derivatives at $x = a$, and read derivatives straight off a polynomial's coefficients.

beforeThis.skill: Shortcut: the number sitting in front of $(x - a)^k$ in a Taylor polynomial is always $\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}$. Multiply that coefficient by $k!$ to get $f^{(k)}(a)$ instantly!

seeIt.title: Taylor series (Ch. 11 of Essence of Calculus)
seeIt.creator: 3Blue1Brown
seeIt.watchFor: Shows how each $k$th derivative at $x = a$ determines the coefficient $\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}$ of $(x - a)^k$.

slowWalkthrough.title: Calculus 2 Lecture 9.9: Approximation of Functions by Taylor Polynomials
slowWalkthrough.creator: Professor Leonard

questions.asking: Find the numerical value of $f''(1)$ from the given third-degree Taylor polynomial $T_3(x)$ centered at $x = 1$.
questions.statement:
The 3rd degree Taylor polynomial for a function $f(x)$ about $x = 1$ is

$$T_3(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 9x$$

What is $f''(1)$?

questions.asking: Write down the third-degree Maclaurin polynomial $T_3(x)$ by dropping the degree-$4$ term from $T_4(x)$.
questions.statement:
The 4th-degree Maclaurin polynomial for $f(x)$ is

$$T_4(x) = x^4 - x^3 + x^2 - x + 1$$

What is the third-degree Maclaurin polynomial for $f(x)$?
